`networkflow` is a research pipeline for studying networks built from
tabular data. Research data rarely come as networks: they come as tables
of links between two kinds of entities, such as articles and the
references they cite, authors and the papers they sign, or even social media accounts and
what they share. `networkflow` turns such tables into networks, finds the
communities they contain, follows these communities over time, and helps
name, draw and explore them.

The package was written for, and used in, research on the history and
sociology of sciences, where bibliographic coupling networks (articles
linked by the references they share) map the research fronts of a
literature [@kessler1963; @boyack2010].

Its central feature is the
*dynamic* workflow: one network per time window, clusters in each window,
and a rule that links the clusters of successive windows (building "intertemporal" or "dynamic" clusters), 
so that a literature can be seen being born, growing, splitting and fading. Each
step is a documented function whose choices (similarity measure,
threshold, time window, clustering algorithm, resolution, matching rule)
are explicit arguments that can be varied and reported. Everything returns
`tbl_graph` objects from [`tidygraph`](https://tidygraph.data-imaginist.com/), or lists of them, which can be
manipulated with [`dplyr`](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/) and drawn with [`ggraph`](https://ggraph.data-imaginist.com/).

The pipeline is not specific to citations: any table of links between two
kinds of entities can be projected onto one of them. Besides bibliographic
coupling, the guides show co-citation (cited works linked when they are
cited together), the coupling of authors instead of articles, and
co-authorship; the same logic applies to accounts and the hashtags they
use, or to members and the boards they sit on.

## Installation

You can install the development version of `networkflow` from GitHub:

```r
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("agoutsmedt/networkflow")
```

The package imports only what the core pipeline needs. Some steps use
packages that are suggested, not imported, and the function that needs one
asks to install it: [`ggalluvial`](https://corybrunson.github.io/ggalluvial/) for `plot_alluvial()`, [`tidytext`](https://juliasilge.github.io/tidytext/) for the
tf-idf names of `name_clusters()` and `extract_tfidf()`, [`textstem`](https://github.com/trinker/textstem) to
lemmatise terms, [`backbone`](https://github.com/zpneal/backbone) for the statistical backbones (`method = "sdsm"`...), [`ellmer`](https://ellmer.tidyverse.org) for the labels of a language model (`name_clusters(method = "llm")`).

## A first look

The package includes the corpus of @goutsmedt2021: the books and articles
that explained the US stagflation of the 1970s, published between 1975 and
2013, and the references they cite. `build_network()` links two
explanations when they cite the same references (bibliographic coupling),
`add_clusters()` detects groups of explanations that share a literature,
and `name_clusters()` labels each group with the words that distinguish
its titles.

```{r}
#| label: first-look
library(networkflow)

nodes <- subset(Nodes_stagflation, source_type == "Stagflation")

network <- build_network(
  nodes = nodes,
  directed_edges = Ref_stagflation,
  source_id = "source_id",
  target_id = "target_id",
  method = "similarity",
  edges_threshold = 1
)

network <- add_clusters(
  network,
  clustering_method = "leiden",
  objective_function = "modularity",
  seed = 123,
  verbose = FALSE
)

network <- name_clusters(
  network,
  method = "tf-idf",
  cluster_id = "cluster_leiden",
  text_columns = "source_title",
  nb_terms_label = 3,
  clean_word_method = "lemmatize"
)
```

`layout_networks()`, `color_networks()` and `plot_networks()` then draw it:

```{r}
#| label: first-plot
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
# The figure comes in a light and a dark version, so that it follows the
# theme of the website (see `.only-light` / `.only-dark` in
# pkgdown/extra.scss). The code is hidden: the call is the one shown above.
# Both versions have a transparent background; the dark one only changes
# the outline of the nodes. On GitHub, the `#gh-*-mode-only` suffixes do the
# same job as the CSS classes.
withr::local_seed(1)
network <- layout_networks(network, node_id = "source_id", layout = "fr")
network <- color_networks(network, column_to_color = "cluster_leiden")
fig_alt <- paste(
  "Bibliographic coupling network of the explanations of the 1970s",
  "stagflation, with nodes coloured by cluster and a label made of the",
  "three most distinctive title words of each cluster."
)
for (mode in c("light", "dark")) {
  ggplot2::update_geom_defaults("point", list(colour = if (mode == "dark") "#F1EDE2" else "black"))
  p <- plot_networks(network, cluster_label_column = "cluster_label", node_size_column = NULL)
  ggplot2::ggsave(
    sprintf("man/figures/README-first-plot-%s.png", mode), p,
    width = 10, height = 8, dpi = 150, bg = "transparent"
  )
}
ggplot2::update_geom_defaults("point", list(colour = "black"))
cat(
  sprintf('<img src="man/figures/README-first-plot-%s.png#gh-%s-mode-only" class="only-%s" alt="%s" width="100%%">',
          c("light", "dark"), c("light", "dark"), c("light", "dark"), fig_alt),
  sep = "\n"
)
```

The clusters already sketch the history that @goutsmedt2021 tells:
explanations of the late 1970s centred on productivity, oil and wages, and
a literature of the 2000s on the "great inflation" and monetary policy
rules. The guides below show how to follow this change window by window.

## Guides

Five guides, written around the same example, follow the steps of a
study. Each explains the method behind the step, with the literature it
comes from, before showing the code.

- [From references to networks](https://agoutsmedt.github.io/networkflow/articles/from-references-to-networks.html)
  explains what a projected network is, how bibliographic coupling is
  measured, which threshold or statistical backbone to choose, and how to
  cut a corpus into time windows.
- [Finding and reading clusters](https://agoutsmedt.github.io/networkflow/articles/finding-and-reading-clusters.html)
  presents community detection with the Leiden algorithm, the role of the
  resolution and of the random seed, and how to name clusters and characterise
  the role of their members.
- [Drawing networks](https://agoutsmedt.github.io/networkflow/articles/drawing-networks.html)
  explains what a layout does and compares the force-directed layouts
  (Fruchterman-Reingold, Kamada-Kawai, ForceAtlas2) with UMAP, then shows how to
  colour, label and draw the clusters.
- [Following clusters over time](https://agoutsmedt.github.io/networkflow/articles/following-clusters-over-time.html)
  links the clusters of successive windows into dynamic clusters and draws
  their history as an alluvial plot.
- [Beyond bibliographic coupling](https://agoutsmedt.github.io/networkflow/articles/beyond-bibliographic-coupling.html)
  uses the same pipeline for co-citation, for authors instead of
  articles and for any two-mode table, and explains why the identifiers of
  references matter.

## What is in the package

**Building networks.** `build_network()` and `build_dynamic_networks()`
project a two-mode table (e.g. articles and their references) onto a
network of the first entities, for the whole corpus or one network per
time window (in years, months or days, sliding by any step). Ties are weighted with one of the five bibliometric similarity measures of
[`biblionetwork`](https://agoutsmedt.github.io/biblionetwork/) [@goutsmedt2023biblionetwork], or kept only when they are
statistically significant under a null model, with the [`backbone`](https://github.com/zpneal/backbone) package
[@neal2022]. `filter_components()` keeps the main component(s).

**Finding and reading clusters.** `add_clusters()` detects communities with
Leiden [@traag2019], Louvain, Infomap, walktrap or fast greedy.
`merge_dynamic_clusters()` links the clusters of successive windows, and
`merge_diagnostics()` shows how the result depends on the threshold.
`name_clusters()` and `extract_tfidf()` describe them by their most
distinctive words or most central members, and `add_node_roles()` places
each node with the within-module degree and participation coefficient of
@guimera2005.

**Drawing and exploring.** `layout_networks()` computes coordinates, with
an option to keep them stable across windows; `color_networks()`,
`prepare_label_networks()` and `plot_networks()` draw networks;
`networks_to_alluv()`, `minimize_crossing_alluvial()` and `plot_alluvial()`
draw the history of dynamic clusters.

The [reference](https://agoutsmedt.github.io/networkflow/reference/index.html)
lists every function.

## Speed

`bench/benchmark_functions.R` runs the dynamic pipeline (six sliding
five-year windows) on samples of a Scopus corpus of economics articles
(1995-2004) and compares it with the former version of the package. On
20,000 articles, building the six networks takes about 26 s and 1.1 GB,
and Leiden with a fixed 1,000 iterations (the former default) about 200 s.
The default is now `n_iterations = -1` (iterate until the partition is
stable), which gives the same modularity in a fraction of that time. Colouring edges is now about 90
times faster (0.7 s instead of 59 s). The other steps take a few seconds,
and the results are identical to those of the former version, except for
the intended changes listed in `NEWS.md`.

## Research using networkflow

`networkflow` grew out of, and was used in, the following studies:

- @goutsmedt2021 on the explanations of the 1970s US stagflation, whose
  data are the examples of the package;
- @goutsmedt2023eer on European macroeconomics and the *European Economic
  Review*;
- @delcey2027dissemination on the bibliometric analysis of the dissemination of
  Fama (1970);
- @delcey2026 on the history of rationality in economic thought;
- @duluins2026 on the scientific reception of the *Livestock's Long
  Shadow* report;
- the [Digital History of Macroeconomics](https://www.digitalhistoryofscience.org/dhm/)
  project [@goutsmedt2025dhm], which maps the macroeconomics literature
  since the 1970s and whose deliverable is archived on Zenodo;
- @boucher2025 on productivity and citations in the field of contemporary
  China studies.

## Authors

`networkflow` was developed by Aurélien Goutsmedt, Thomas
Delcey and Alexandre Truc. Alexandre Truc initiated the alluvial method for following clusters
over time (`networks_to_alluv()`, `minimize_crossing_alluvial()`,
`plot_alluvial()`). The package is maintained by Thomas Delcey and Aurélien
Goutsmedt.
